entry: 2012 [[Documentary film|documentary]] directed by Joshua Oppenheimer, with Christine Cynn and an anonymous Indonesian co-director. It follows perpetrators of the Indonesian mass killings of 1965–66, who re-enact their murders in cinematic styles drawn from gangster films and westerns. Filmed mostly in [[Medan]], North Sumatra, it premiered at the Telluride Film Festival in 2012 and received widespread critical acclaim, including a British Academy Film Award. The Indonesian government has claimed that it is a misleading portrayal of the country's history. Its spiritual successor, *The Look of Silence* (2014), depicts a victim's family confronting the killers.

Fictional family and franchise created by American cartoonist Charles Addams. Its eccentric, old-money clan first appeared in single-panel cartoons in *The New Yorker* in 1938. Adaptations include a live-action ABC television series from 1964, 1990s feature films, animated series, and a 2010 Broadway musical. Netflix's *Wednesday* (2022) centers on the family's daughter. The family has influenced American comics, cinema and television, as well as the [[Goth subculture]].

Series of 24 comic albums by Belgian cartoonist [[Hergé]]. It debuted in 1929 in *Le Petit Vingtième*, a youth supplement to a Belgian newspaper, and follows Tintin, a young Belgian reporter and adventurer, and his dog Snowy. Their adventures mix fantasy, mystery, political thriller and science fiction, with slapstick humor and dashes of political or cultural commentary. Hergé drew the series in a precise, uniform outline style known as *ligne claire* ("clear line"). Early volumes, including *Tintin in the Congo*, have been criticized for colonial-era stereotypes, and Hergé revised some content in later editions. The series has been adapted for radio, television, theatre and film, including [[Steven Spielberg]]'s 2011 motion-capture film.

Philosophical novel by Brazilian author Paulo Coelho, first published in 1988. It follows Santiago, an [[Andalusia|Andalusian]] shepherd boy who dreams of treasure at the Egyptian pyramids and travels across North Africa to find it. Along the way he meets [[Melchizedek]], the king of Salem, and an alchemist who teaches him to pursue his "Personal Legend." The plot builds on an international folktale about treasure found at home. Written in Portuguese, the novel became an international bestseller, with more than 150 million copies sold worldwide.

Series of three Bengali-language films directed by [[Satyajit Ray]], released between 1955 and 1959: *Pather Panchali*, *Aparajito* and *The World of Apu*. Adapted from two novels by Bibhutibhushan Bandopadhyay, the films follow Apu, a young Bengali, from childhood to early maturity in the early 20th century. Made on a modest budget with an amateur cast, the trilogy won three National Film Awards and honors at the [[Cannes Film Festival|Cannes]], Berlin and Venice film festivals. Its score was composed by [[Ravi Shankar]]. Ray decided to go ahead with the first film after meeting [[Jean Renoir]] and watching the Italian neorealist film *Bicycle Thieves* (1948) in London. The trilogy is widely regarded as a cornerstone of Indian and world cinema.

Ancient Chinese military treatise of 13 chapters, traditionally attributed to the general [[Sun Tzu]]. Its authorship is disputed, and its earliest parts probably date to at least a century after Sun Tzu is said to have lived. The treatise covers weapons, terrain, financial logistics, morale, rank and discipline. It portrays war as a costly, destructive last resort and stresses diplomacy, economic principles, and the value of intelligence operatives and espionage. The first European-language translation appeared in 1772, and the first annotated English translation in 1910. Leaders who have cited it include Chinese communist revolutionary [[Mao Zedong]], Vietnamese general [[Võ Nguyên Giáp]] and American general [[Douglas MacArthur]]. For almost 1,500 years it was the lead text in the anthology later formalized as the Seven Military Classics.

[[Ancient Greek]] [[Tragedy|tragedy]] by [[Euripides]], written during the playwright's final years at the court of Archelaus I of Macedon. It premiered posthumously in 405 BC at the Theatre of Dionysus in Athens, where it won first prize at the City Dionysia. The play tells how the god [[Dionysus]] takes revenge on Thebes after its king, Pentheus, rejects his cult. Dionysus drives the women of the city into ecstatic frenzy, and Pentheus, lured to the mountains, is torn apart by them, including his own mother, Agave. Regarded as Euripides' masterpiece, it is distinctive for integrating the chorus into the plot and for making the god a central character.

Archipelagic country of more than 700 islands in the Atlantic Ocean, southeast of [[Florida]] and north of [[Cuba]], considered part of the wider Caribbean region. Its capital and largest city is Nassau, on New Providence Island. The islands were inhabited by the Lucayans, a branch of the [[Taíno]], until [[Christopher Columbus]] made the first European landfall in the New World in 1492. Spain shipped the Lucayans to [[Hispaniola]] and enslaved them, leaving the islands mostly deserted from 1513 until 1648. The Bahamas became a crown colony of the [[Kingdom of Great Britain]] in 1718, when the British clamped down on [[Piracy]]. Slavery was abolished in 1834, and African slaves and their descendants became the majority. The Bahamas became independent from the United Kingdom in 1973, keeping King Charles III as monarch. Its economy depends on [[Tourism]] and offshore finance.

American rock band formed in Hawthorne, California, in 1961 by brothers [[Brian Wilson]], Dennis and Carl Wilson, their cousin Mike Love and Al Jardine. Known for vocal harmonies and songs about [[Surfing|surfing]] and youth culture in [[Southern California]], the group had 16 consecutive U.S. top 40 hit singles in a five-year streak. Under Brian Wilson's leadership it moved toward orchestral, studio-focused pop, producing the 1966 album *Pet Sounds* and the single "Good Vibrations," which are widely regarded as among the most influential works in popular music history. Dennis Wilson drowned in 1983, and Carl Wilson died of [[Lung cancer]] in 1998. The founding members were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1988. The band has sold more than 100 million records worldwide.

Ninth studio album and only double album by the English rock band [[The Beatles]], released in November 1968. Commonly called *The White Album* for its plain white sleeve, it has a fragmentary style and draws on folk, country rock, blues, ska and hard rock. 19 of its 30 songs were written in India in 1968, and the recording sessions were marked by tension, including the presence of [[Yoko Ono]] and the temporary departure of [[Ringo Starr]]. It topped the charts in Britain and the United States and has been certified 24× platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America.

Only novel by American writer and poet [[Sylvia Plath]], first published in London in 1963 under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas. Semi-autobiographical, it follows Esther Greenwood, a student from the [[Boston]] suburbs whose summer internship at a [[New York City]] magazine is followed by a mental breakdown. Plath died by [[Suicide]] a month after the novel's first British publication. It was published under her name in 1966, and it was not published in the United States until 1971, in line with the wishes of her husband Ted Hughes and her mother. It has been translated into more than 40 languages.

American [[Sitcom|sitcom]] created by [[Chuck Lorre]] and Bill Prady for [[CBS]], broadcast from 2007 to 2019 for 12 seasons and 279 episodes. Filmed before a live audience, it centers on Leonard Hofstadter, an experimental physicist, and his roommate Sheldon Cooper, a theoretical physicist who researches [[Quantum mechanics]] and [[String theory]] at the California Institute of Technology. Their neighbor Penny is a waitress and aspiring actress. Jim Parsons won four Emmy Awards for playing Sheldon. The show spawned the prequel *Young Sheldon* (2017–2024) and other spin-offs.

1998 crime comedy film written and directed by the [[Coen brothers]], starring [[Jeff Bridges]] as Jeffrey Lebowski, known as The Dude, a Los Angeles slacker who is mistaken for a millionaire with the same name and drawn into a kidnapping scheme. Loosely inspired by [[Raymond Chandler]], the neo-noir film received mixed reviews on its release. Its eccentric characters, comedic dream sequences and eclectic soundtrack later earned it a cult following. In 2014 it was selected for preservation in the National Film Registry by the [[Library of Congress]].

Painting by [[Sandro Botticelli]], probably executed in the mid-1480s, showing the goddess [[Venus (mythology)|Venus]] arriving on the shore after her birth from the sea. She stands nude on a giant [[Scallop]] shell as the wind god Zephyrus blows her toward land, and a Hora holds a cloak to cover her. The painting is in the [[Uffizi]] Gallery in [[Florence]]. Its large scale and the prominence of its nude female figure were virtually unprecedented in Western art since classical antiquity. The title *Birth of Venus* was applied only in the 19th century, although Vasari had identified the subject. Its appeal is sensory and accessible, and its main meaning is a straightforward treatment of a Greek mythological scene.

1915 American silent epic drama film directed by [[D. W. Griffith]] and starring [[Lillian Gish]]. Adapted from Thomas Dixon Jr.'s 1905 novel and play *The Clansman*, it follows two families, one Northern and one Southern, through the [[American Civil War]] and [[Reconstruction era|Reconstruction]], and it depicts the assassination of [[Abraham Lincoln]] by [[John Wilkes Booth]]. Lauded for its technical virtuosity, it was the first non-serial American 12-reel film and was screened at the White House for President [[Woodrow Wilson]]. It was denounced for its racist depiction of African Americans, with white actors in blackface, and for portraying the [[Ku Klux Klan]] as heroic. Black leaders and the NAACP campaigned unsuccessfully to ban it, even as it grossed more than any previous motion picture. The Library of Congress selected it for preservation in 1992.

Third studio album by the American rock band [[My Chemical Romance]], released in 2006. A concept album, it follows a man with terminal cancer known as The Patient as he nears the end of his life. It is considered [[Emo]] with elements of [[Alternative rock]] and [[Punk rock]]. The album debuted at number two on the Billboard 200. Its lead single, "Welcome to the Black Parade," was the band's first number-one single in the United Kingdom. It is widely regarded as one of the most important works in emo, and *Rolling Stone* ranked it number 361 among the 500 greatest albums of all time.

1999 American found footage horror film written, edited and directed by Daniel Myrick and Eduardo Sánchez. Presented as a pseudo-documentary, it follows three film students who hike into the [[Appalachian Mountains]] near Burkittsville, [[Maryland]], to investigate a local legend and disappear. The actors were listed as missing or deceased in the film's marketing. It premiered at the Sundance [[Film festival|Film Festival]] in January 1999, and Artisan Entertainment acquired its distribution rights for $1.1 million. Grossing $248.6 million worldwide, it became one of the most successful independent films of all time and revived the found footage technique.

Bombing campaign by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy against the [[United Kingdom]] during the Second World War, from September 7, 1940, to May 16, 1941. Its name is a shortened form of *Blitzkrieg*, meaning lightning war. After the [[Battle of Britain]], the Luftwaffe systematically bombed [[London]] for 56 of 57 days, then shifted to night raids on cities including [[Liverpool]], [[Coventry]] and Manchester. More than 40,000 civilians were killed in Luftwaffe bombing during the war. The campaign did not force British surrender or seriously hamper war production, although British studies found that most severely hit cities took 10 to 15 days to recover.

Photograph of [[Earth]] taken on December 7, 1972, by one of the astronauts aboard the [[NASA]] Apollo 17 spacecraft on its way to the [[Moon]]. Taken from about 29,400 kilometers (18,300 mi) away, the image shows Earth from the [[Mediterranean Sea]] to Antarctica. It was the first time that the Apollo trajectory and seasonal timing made it possible to photograph the south polar ice cap. Africa, Madagascar, the Arabian Peninsula and most of the Indian Ocean are visible. A cropped, rotated and processed version has become one of the most reproduced images in history. NASA has also applied the name to a 2012 series of composite images covering the entire globe.

Scientific and philosophical encyclopedia by Avicenna, begun in 1014, completed around 1020 and published in 1027. Intended to cure ignorance of the soul, it is not concerned with medicine, which is treated in the separate [[The Canon of Medicine]]. The book is divided into four parts: [[Logic]], natural sciences, [[Mathematics]] and [[Metaphysics]]. It was influenced by [[Aristotle]], [[Ptolemy]] and earlier thinkers such as [[Al-Kindi]]. In astronomy, it proposes that Venus is closer to Earth than the Sun. It also offers a theory of petrifying fluids to explain fossils. Avicenna was the first to divide human perception into five external and five internal senses, and he described the effect of emotions on the body.

headword: The Bridge on the River Kwai
entry: Epic war film directed by [[David Lean]] and based on Pierre Boulle's novel. Set during the construction of the Burma Railway in 1942–1943, it follows British prisoners of war forced to build a bridge for their Japanese captors. [[Alec Guinness]] and [[William Holden]] star. The blacklisted screenwriters Carl Foreman and Michael Wilson worked in secret, and Boulle, who did not speak English, received the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Adapted Screenplay. The film won seven Academy Awards, including Best Picture, and was the highest-grossing film of 1957.

Northernmost of the five boroughs of [[New York City]] and the only one located primarily on the U.S. mainland. Coextensive with Bronx County, it had 1,472,654 residents at the 2020 census and covers 42 square miles. The name derives from Jonas Bronck, who established the first European settlement there in 1639. Immigrants from Ireland, Germany, Italy and Eastern Europe were followed by migrants from [[Puerto Rico]], Jamaica and the [[Dominican Republic]]. The South Bronx suffered severe urban decay from the 1960s to the 1990s. The borough is home to Yankee Stadium of [[Major League Baseball]] and is the birthplace of [[Hip-hop]].

Final novel by Russian author [[Fyodor Dostoevsky]], serialized in *The Russian Messenger* from January 1879 to November 1880. Set in 19th-century Russia, it centers on the murder of the family patriarch, Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov, and asks who is guilty. Its discussion of God, free will and morality has been described as a theological drama about faith, doubt and reason in a modernizing Russia. Dostoevsky composed much of the novel in Staraya Russa, which inspired its setting. His three-year-old son had died of [[Epilepsy]] in 1878, and the grief is apparent throughout the book. Dostoevsky died less than four months after publication. Thinkers influenced by the novel include [[Sigmund Freud]] and [[Albert Einstein]].

American commercial broadcast television network that debuted on September 18, 2006, as a successor to UPN and the WB. Its name combines the first letters of its founding co-owners, [[CBS]] and Warner Bros. Programming aims mainly at viewers aged 18 to 34 and has included the long-running [[Supernatural (American TV series)|Supernatural]]. Nexstar Media Group acquired a controlling stake in 2022. Its lineup has expanded to include WWE and NASCAR programming.

Medical encyclopedia in five books, compiled by Avicenna and completed in 1025. It presents the medical knowledge of the Islamic world, which had been influenced by [[Galen]] and by earlier Greco-Roman, Persian, Chinese and Indian medicine. Avicenna sought to fit Galen's tradition, and thereby that of [[Hippocrates]], into [[Aristotle]]'s natural philosophy. Written in [[Arabic]], it was translated into [[Latin]] in 12th-century Toledo and became a standard textbook for teaching in European universities into the early modern period. It also set the standards for medicine in medieval Europe and the Islamic world, and it remained a standard textbook through the 18th century in Europe. It is an important text in Unani medicine, a traditional medicine practiced in India.
